summary: The week the engine became neutral: one language (gkql), no domain words in the core, and use cases moved outside it. The paper now defines what the engine does before it is built. The cost was high: the rules for time and late data changed three times, and reviews and hand-overs took a large share of the effort.

areas.name: Paper
areas.about: The math-first definition of graphs, changes and time that the engine has to follow.

areas.name: Engine
areas.about: The runtime that turns incoming changes into updated graphs, and its one language, gkql.

areas.name: Use cases
areas.about: Real applications written only in gkql and run outside the engine: the Azure health model, its policy rules and the data collectors.

areas.name: Canvas
areas.about: The browser views: the graph canvas, the gkql editor and this review site.

areas.name: Running the work
areas.about: How the sessions were organised: issues, decisions, hand-overs, reviews and the tools around them.

days.note: Only the architecture feedback board was built. It was parked the next day.
Andre reset the plan: paper first, then engine, then use cases. gkql became the only language, the core went neutral and the old paper chapters were replaced.
The busiest day: gkql completed, the health model rebuilt outside the engine, collectors added, and the rules for folding windows over time changed twice.
Late data reopened the time chapter. Then Andre stopped new work for this review.

themes.title: A new core paper replaced the old chapters
themes.what: The chapters were written from the problem statement to related work: values and identity, graphs, how changes combine, runs, and time. The old chapters were removed and their links point to the new ones.
themes.why: Paper first: the engine and its tests must follow a definition that has been checked, not the other way round.

themes.title: The time chapter was rewritten for late data
themes.what: First a keyed fold over windows was defined, then a carried start state at its look-back edge, then a rule for when a key may be dropped. On the last day Andre decided that no input is dropped for being late: the chapter now says late input revises what it reaches and old windows move to storage instead of being forgotten.
themes.why: Historic, new and late data must give the same result whatever order they arrive in.

themes.title: gkql became the only language
themes.what: The two older ways to write definitions were removed in one cut. Every operator the shipped definitions use can now be written in gkql, and all definitions and fixtures were ported with neutral names.
themes.why: Two languages meant two meanings to prove, test and teach. One language is smaller.

themes.title: The core no longer knows any domain
themes.what: All input now arrives in one record envelope. The code that understood Azure, pods or health left the runtime and the command line, and a guard test fails the build if a domain word comes back.
themes.why: Use cases belong in projections written in gkql, not in the engine.

themes.title: gkql covers every requirement of the paper
themes.what: Recursion over edges (a least value per node), percentile, exact sums, a state that holds until a change is confirmed, and lateness declared per input. A conformance list records each requirement and where gkql meets it.
themes.why: The language had to express every use case before the use cases were rebuilt on it.

themes.title: One keyed fold over windows replaced the threshold operator
themes.what: A single fold walks each key's windows in time order and carries a state. It replaced a special threshold operator, and its cost now follows the changes, not the size of the history.
themes.why: Policies such as 'unhealthy for three windows' are then plain gkql in a library, not engine code.

themes.title: The host keeps its lifecycle to itself
themes.what: The phase of a running space is private to the host; tests read what the host serves instead of its insides.
themes.why: An architecture review found the host was becoming the owner of everything under one lock.

themes.title: The Azure health model was rebuilt outside the engine
themes.what: All 47 signals of the deployed model are computed in gkql from raw data and compared with two settled checkpoints of the real model. Names that could identify resources are replaced by keyed aliases.
themes.why: Proof that a real use case runs on the neutral engine without engine changes.

themes.title: Health policy became a gkql library
themes.what: The rules that turn signals into states (for example, how long a signal must stay bad) are a library over the keyed fold.
themes.why: Policy is data the user can read and change, not engine code.

shots.caption: The developer guide shows a health rule as a fold over one-minute CPU windows with four plain settings: above, below, enter after and exit after.

themes.title: Collectors bring data in from outside
themes.what: Logs, platform metrics through Event Hubs, Prometheus samples and Kubernetes metrics are read by collectors that write record envelopes. The tutorial got its own collector.
themes.why: The engine reads records only; every source-specific detail stays outside it.

shots.caption: The tutorial on record envelopes: a first projection turns captured pod calls into calls between services, and each call can be traced to its source.

themes.title: The KQL editor became a gkql editor
themes.what: The old KQL editor was removed. The new editor shows the steps, the graph and the text of one gkql program in step, with undo, and its checking is one explicit state machine.
themes.why: Users edit the one language the engine runs.

shots.caption: The new gkql editor: the steps of one projection on the left, the same steps as a graph in the middle, the selected step on the right. The engine accepts the draft as it is.

themes.title: A design pass on the Canvas
themes.what: Neutral badges, colour only for states, readable legends, a status bar with user readouts and renderer colours that match the drawing sheet.
themes.why: Colour should carry meaning, not decoration.

shots.caption: The data graph after the design pass: plain type list with counts, colour only on types and states, readouts in the status bar.

themes.title: The Canvas followed each engine change
themes.what: It reads the neutral record envelope, the new event and window names and the keyed fold.
themes.why: Every engine wire change needs a matching Canvas change the same day.

themes.title: Work moved to managed sessions on one checkout
themes.what: An orchestrator starts worker sessions, one issue each, all on main. Each issue has numbered acceptance criteria; workers post proof, an independent review checks it and only the orchestrator closes. A board mirrors the issues.
themes.why: Several sessions could work at once without branches, and every claim has a link.

themes.title: Rules to cut the cost of the run
themes.what: After a token audit: one issue per session, idle sessions wait for mail instead of polling, the test reference is written before the engine change, reviews look only at the diff, and cheaper models for searches and small reviews.
themes.why: The first full day of the run used about 76 million tokens.

waste.title: The rules for time changed three times in two days
waste.plain: The keyed fold was defined, then given a carried start state, then a rule for dropping keys, each time through paper, test reference and engine. A day later Andre decided that nothing is dropped for being late, which removed the carried state from the paper. The engine work for the new rule is still open.
waste.cost: 3 issues of paper, reference and engine work, about 900 changed lines and at least 11 million input-equivalent tokens in the sessions started for them, now partly replaced

evidence.label: Decision: no input is dropped for being late

waste.suggestion: Settle a time rule with Andre in the paper, with a worked example of late data, before the reference and the engine start.

waste.title: One issue took 18 review rounds, another 13
waste.plain: The policy library went back and forth between failing and passing reviews 18 times. The audit found the cause: the engine session wrote its own test reference and copied its own mistakes into it. The gkql completeness issue drew 13 rounds and 40 comments.
waste.cost: 31 review rounds on two issues, about 124,000 characters of comments

evidence.label: Token audit: the cause of the five extra reviews

waste.suggestion: Keep the rule from the audit: a different session writes the reference from the paper first. After three failed rounds, split the issue.

waste.title: Memory was checked after the engine was built
waste.plain: One fold key over six hours used about 142 KB, more than the memory budget allows. It was found after the fold was finished, which led to the note on draining old windows and the rewrite of the time chapter.
waste.cost: One extra issue and a research note before the next engine step
waste.suggestion: Keep the budget check, but run it on the paper's worked example before the engine is built.

waste.title: 11,617 lines landed without an issue
waste.plain: A large set of health mirror diagnostics and scripts was committed with no issue. Two later review fixes removed parts of it again, a test file and a capture.
waste.cost: 11,617 lines, of which parts were removed in two review fixes
waste.suggestion: No commit without an issue; large lab drops go in under the issue that needs them.

waste.title: A feedback board was built and parked the next day
waste.plain: A 5,669-line architecture board that wrote feedback back to GitHub was built on the first evening; the plan was reset the next day and the board is parked. This site replaces it.
waste.suggestion: Build a tool when a question needs it; read GitHub instead of writing to it.

waste.title: One change was reverted and redone
waste.plain: A rule for when a series starts was changed in the engine, reverted the same day and redone with a different rule.
waste.suggestion: A quick revert is cheap; keep doing it. The cause was an engine change ahead of the paper.

overdone.title: Full reviews of renames and one-line paper edits found nothing
overdone.plain: A rename of graph names, a rename of time series to events and windows, and a one-paragraph paper fix each got a full independent review with an engine test run. All three passed at the first round with nothing found.
overdone.cost: 3 review sessions with full test runs; all reviews ran as orchestrator subagents, 16 million input-equivalent tokens over the week
overdone.suggestion: For renames and sentence edits, the orchestrator checks the diff itself; keep full reviews for new behaviour.

overdone.title: Criteria kept moving between issues
overdone.plain: At least seven acceptance criteria moved from one issue to another during the week, for example from the language-complete issue to the health model rebuild, from the health model to the lateness issue, and from the fold memory issue to the open drain issue. The health model rebuild ended with nine criteria and the neutral-core epic with ten.
overdone.cost: 7 or more moved criteria; two issues with nine and ten criteria
overdone.suggestion: Turn a moved criterion into a new small issue, and split an issue with more than eight criteria before work starts.

overdone.title: Documents that nothing links to
overdone.plain: The gkql conformance list changed in 20 commits but no file links to it, and it repeats part of the paper. The research note on fold memory was turned into the time chapter the same day. A 412-line analysis of the health mirror is linked from nowhere.
overdone.cost: 20 commits to one unlinked list; a note and a chapter saying the same thing
overdone.suggestion: Write a change into the chapter directly, and link or fold the conformance list into the paper.

overdone.title: The protocol document changed in 26 commits
overdone.plain: Engine steps edited the protocol document 26 times in three days. The same five engine files changed in 14 to 24 commits each, across many issues.
overdone.cost: 26 commits to one file in three days
overdone.suggestion: Update the protocol once per finished issue, not per commit.

overdone.title: Running the sessions cost more than the work in them
overdone.plain: Over the week 57 sessions used 183 million input-equivalent tokens and 8.2 million output tokens. 85% of the input side was re-reading context already in the cache. Turns with more than 250,000 tokens of context carried a quarter of the input side. The orchestrator and its subagents, which ran the reviews, took 41 million (23%). Almost all of it, 98.6%, ran on the largest model. In three days there were 8 orchestrator and 26 worker hand-overs.
overdone.cost: 183 million input-equivalent tokens; 41 million for orchestration and reviews; 34 hand-overs

evidence.label: Token audit of the first full day
Decision: models by kind of work

overdone.suggestion: Keep the audit's rules and the cheaper models; measure again at the end of next week.

overdone.title: The rules of the run changed five times in three days
overdone.plain: Five decisions changed how sessions work. One of them forbade the slow test runs that earlier hand-overs had told workers to run, so those hand-overs were wrong the moment they were read.
overdone.cost: 5 rule changes; stale instructions in earlier hand-overs
overdone.suggestion: Collect rule changes and apply them once a day, in the briefs, not in hand-overs.

overdone.title: The same pitfall was written in nine hand-overs
overdone.plain: How the shell splits file paths for a commit was explained again in nine worker hand-overs instead of being fixed once.
overdone.suggestion: Put it into the common rules or a small commit helper once.

good.title: Use cases left the engine
good.plain: The health model, its policy and the collectors run in gkql outside the engine, and a guard keeps domain words out of it.

good.title: The old plan was cleared
good.plain: 21 issues from the old plan were closed on the day of the reset, so the board lists only live work.

good.title: Every claim has a link
good.plain: Acceptance criteria with ids and proof per criterion made it possible to write this review from the issues alone.

tokens.method: Summed from the Claude Code session transcripts of this project: every model reply records its tokens, and each reply is counted once. A day runs on Central European time. The kind of a session comes from the brief it was started with; subagents count to the session that started them. Sessions started with a general brief (engine, paper, canvas, lab, orchestrator) worked on several issues, so only sessions started for one issue are counted per issue.
tokens.weights: Input-equivalent counts new input and cache writes in full and a cache read at one tenth, the rough price ratio. Output is shown apart.
